passage:
Monday. Rajni got 14 out of 25 in chemistry and snapped at her little sister for humming. By evening she was sure her friends thought she was stupid.
Wednesday. A pimple on her chin. She wore her hair over her face all day and skipped the lunch table. Her friend Sonali texted, "u ok?" Rajni typed "fine" and then cried in the bathroom, not even sure why.
Saturday. She laughed through a whole film with Sonali, then felt low again at bedtime. Her mother found her awake and sat down. "Up and down this week?" Rajni nodded. "That's very common at fifteen. We'll keep an eye on it together. If it ever starts stopping you from school or friends, we'll talk to someone who helps with this." Rajni leaned on her shoulder.

qa.q: What did Rajni score in chemistry?
qa.a: Rajni got 14 out of 25 in chemistry.

qa.q: What did Rajni believe about her friends on Monday evening?
qa.a: She was sure her friends thought she was stupid, a doubt that grew out of one test mark.

qa.q: What did Rajni's mother do on Saturday night that helped?
qa.a: She named the ups and downs calmly, said they are common, and agreed to watch them together and get help if they ever stop daily life.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when Rajni texted "fine" and skipped lunch?
qa.a: Sonali may have felt worried and unsure, sensing something was wrong but not being let in.

grounding: Over a week a teenager swings between irritation, worry and low confidence about marks, looks and friends, and her mother treats it as common while watching for more.

passage: Rukmini, you think you're the only one who wants to hide under a blanket one hour and throw a pillow the next? At fourteen I once cried because my plait was uneven, and an hour later I shouted at my father for asking about homework. I hated my voice, my nose, my maths marks, sometimes all at once. Your Chandrika Masi was a storm. My Amma would wait until it passed, and then she would bring tea and ask, "Big storm or small storm today?" Most were small. One winter they weren't; I stopped wanting to go to school at all, and Amma took me to talk to a counsellor. That helped a lot. So, beta, is today a big storm or a small one?

qa.q: What made Chandrika cry at fourteen?
qa.a: Her plait was uneven.

qa.q: How did young Chandrika feel about herself at fourteen?
qa.a: She was full of self-doubt, hating her voice, her nose and her maths marks, sometimes all at once.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's Amma do when the storms got too big one winter?
qa.a: When Chandrika stopped wanting to go to school at all, Amma took her to talk to a counsellor, which helped.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's Amma have felt, waiting for each storm to pass?
qa.a: Amma was probably patient but watchful, trusting most storms would pass while staying close enough to see when one winter was bigger.

grounding: An aunt tells Rukmini about her own teenage mood swings and self-doubt, and how help came when it stopped daily life.

passage: Anand came home from school, dropped his bag in the hall of the Kolkata flat and snapped at his cousin Rehana for sitting in 'his' chair. Ten minutes later he was laughing at a video. Ten minutes after that he was at the bathroom mirror, glaring at a spot on his chin, muttering that he looked disgusting. At dinner he pushed his rice around. 'Maths result tomorrow. I'll fail. And Sayan hasn't replied all day, so he probably hates me.' Rehana, home from college for the Puja holidays, didn't tease him. 'That's a lot of weather for one evening.' He almost smiled. 'Everything's just annoying.' 'I remember that age. It swings like mad.' She paused. 'But if it ever stops you sleeping or going to school, tell me or your Ma, okay? We'd get you proper help.' He nodded, chewing slowly.

qa.q: What did Anand snap at Rehana about?
qa.a: Sitting in 'his' chair.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Anand go through that evening?
qa.a: He swung from irritation to laughter to feeling disgusted with his looks, then worried about his result and afraid Sayan hated him.

qa.q: What did Rehana get right?
qa.a: She didn't tease, named the swings kindly as common at his age, and asked him to tell her or his Ma if they ever stopped his sleep or school, so he'd get proper help.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rehana to be snapped at, then confided in?
qa.a: Rehana may have been a little stung at first, but stayed patient, seeing the snapping as part of his changing moods.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging between irritation, worry and self-doubt about looks, grades and friends, and a cousin who treats it as common while naming when to get help.

passage:
'Mridul? Can I come in?'
'Whatever.'
Tanuja sat on the end of the bed. 'You slammed the door hard enough to shake the photos.'
'Because everything's stupid. I'm stupid. I got 12 out of 30 in science. And my hair looks like a broom.'
'Yesterday you were singing in the shower.'
'Yesterday was yesterday!'
'Fair.' She waited. 'Still going to football?'
'Yes.'
'Sleeping okay? Eating with us?'
'Mostly. Why?'
'Because moods going up and down like this are really common at fourteen. A lot is changing fast. But if it ever starts stopping you from football, sleep or school, we'll talk to Mrs. D'Souza, the counsellor, together. Deal?'
Mridul pulled the pillow over his face. 'Deal,' he said into it. 'My hair still looks like a broom.'
'A bit like a broom,' she agreed, and he laughed.

qa.q: What did Mridul get in the science test?
qa.a: 12 out of 30.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he called himself stupid?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and low in confidence, upset about the test and his looks.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja ask about football, sleep and eating?
qa.a: To check whether the moods were stopping his daily life; since they weren't, it looked like common teenage swings, with the counsellor as a plan if that changed.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel sitting on the end of Mridul's bed?
qa.a: She was probably a little worried but calm, patient enough to listen and even joke about the broom.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging between irritation and self-doubt over grades and looks, and a parent who treats it as common while checking whether it is stopping daily life.

passage: Looking back at Class 10, I was a weather system. I'm Zeenat. One hour I'd be worrying the board exams would ruin my life, the next I'd be shouting at my brother Tushar for breathing too loudly, the next I'd be sure my friends only put up with me. Mostly it passed. I'd sleep, and the morning would feel lighter. Then in January it didn't pass. I stopped going to tuition, then missed school for three days, lying in bed with my phone and a heaviness I couldn't name. Tushar was the one who noticed. He didn't lecture. He sat on my floor and said, 'This isn't like your usual storms.' That evening he told Ammi, and by the end of the week she had taken me to the school counsellor. I'm glad he said something. I don't think I would have.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when he sat on Zeenat's floor?
qa.a: 'This isn't like your usual storms.'

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel during those January days in bed?
qa.a: Zeenat felt heavy and low, a feeling hard to name, unlike the usual moods that passed with sleep.

qa.q: What made January different, and what was the right response?
qa.a: The low mood stopped daily life, tuition and school, so telling Ammi that evening and seeing the school counsellor was the right step.

qa.q: What might Tushar have felt when he noticed Zeenat staying in bed?
qa.a: He was probably worried, seeing it wasn't Zeenat's usual storms, and chose to speak gently and tell Ammi the same evening.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose common mood swings and self-doubt become a concern when they stop daily life, and the family getting professional help.

passage:
Class teacher's note on Pallavi, Class 10, for my own record.
Monday: Pallavi snapped at Payal over a borrowed pen, then apologised in a whisper.
Tuesday: after the unit test marks, she kept her head down and said, "I'm just bad at everything."
Thursday: laughing with her group, fine in class, and she volunteered to read aloud.
Friday: she asked to skip the class photo because her hair "looked terrible".
Swings like these are very common at this age, and she is still coming to school, finishing work and spending time with friends. I asked her to stay back for two minutes and said, "Some weeks feel up and down. That's allowed." She nodded, eyes wet.
I told her the school counsellor is there if the feelings start getting in the way of sleep, eating or coming to school, and that I'm here too. I will keep watching gently and mention it to her mother at the parent meeting.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi want to skip the class photo?
qa.a: She said her hair "looked terrible".

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling after the unit test marks, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt low and doubtful about herself; she kept her head down and said, "I'm just bad at everything."

qa.q: How did the teacher support Pallavi without making it a big deal?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to her for two minutes, said up-and-down weeks are allowed, and named the counsellor and the teacher as people to go to if it starts getting in the way of daily life.

qa.q: What might Payal have felt when Pallavi snapped at her over a pen?
qa.a: Payal may have been hurt or surprised, but the whispered apology probably helped her see it was about Pallavi's mood, not about her.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a teen's swings between irritation, worry and low confidence, treating them as common while watching for signs they disrupt daily life.
